question.problem:
Given that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $F(x,y)=⟨y+{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},\,x{y}^{2}⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(y+{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})\,dx+x{y}^{2}\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223987/assets/0cb340ef33d4cc38081e3796b4c8e076f1499760c0a3ffeecb8123a41fefeec8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y+{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ and $Q(x,y)=x{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(y+{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})\,dx+x{y}^{2}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}-1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
